paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice 50: The Locked Gate (§B style, standard band)
provenanceNote: NOT STUDENT-FACING. Original narrative written for the morning-quiz bank; NOT from any past exam paper. Section B [19 marks], 1184/02 §B format, SEAB assessment objectives. 10 short-answer items (mixed [1]/[2]) + 4-blank emotion flowchart split for independent auto-grading.

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below about a boy who finds the shortcut through his estate closed off, and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
The gate at the back of Block 214 had been open for as long as anyone could remember. It was not a proper entrance. It was a gap in a fence with a hinge on it, and through it ran a path of beaten earth that saved you nine minutes on the walk to school.

Paragraph 2
On the second Monday of the term there was a chain on it, and a laminated notice, and the nine minutes were gone.

Paragraph 3
We were furious in the way that thirteen-year-olds are furious, which is to say loudly and without any plan. Someone said the town council had done it. Someone else said it was the residents of 214, who had never liked us cutting through. By Wednesday there was a rumour that a boy had been bitten by a dog on the path, and by Thursday the boy had a name, and by Friday he had been bitten twice.

Paragraph 4
My friend Ridzuan was the one who read the notice. The rest of us had walked past it four times without stopping. He came back and told us it said the path was closed for drain works until further notice, and that there was a telephone number on it.

Paragraph 5
We found this disappointing. A drain is not an enemy.

Paragraph 6
Ridzuan called the number. I remember thinking this was an extraordinary thing to do — the number was printed there for adults, surely. He spoke for perhaps ninety seconds, mostly listening, and then thanked the person and hung up.

Paragraph 7
The works would take six weeks. After that the gate would stay locked, because the path crossed land that belonged to the block and the council had been told, by somebody, that children running through at seven in the morning were waking the ground-floor units.

Paragraph 8
So we knew. Knowing did not give us our nine minutes back, and for a week I could not see what it had given us at all.

Paragraph 9
What it gave us was this: on the following Tuesday four of us knocked on three ground-floor doors and asked the residents whether we might use the path if we did not shout. Two doors said no. The third was an old man who said he had never complained about anything in his life and did not intend to start, and who then, unasked, telephoned the council himself.

Paragraph 10
The gate reopened in November with a sign asking users to keep quiet before eight. We kept quiet. I have never in my life been so careful about anything.

Paragraph 11
Ridzuan says he only read the notice because he was early that day and had nothing else to do. I have decided not to believe him.

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, what made the path through the gate valuable to the children? [1]
questions.answer: it cut nine minutes off the walk to school

questions.stem: Q2. Using your own words, explain what the narrator means by being furious 'loudly and without any plan'. (Paragraph 3) [2]
questions.answer: ① their anger was expressed in complaint rather than action; ② nobody thought about what could actually be done, so the noise achieved nothing

questions.stem: Q3. What is the effect of the account of the dog rumour growing from Wednesday to Friday? (Paragraph 3) [2]
questions.answer: the day-by-day escalation shows how quickly an invented explanation gathers convincing detail, and gently mocks the group for preferring a dramatic story to the facts

questions.stem: Q4. What point is the writer making by noting that the others 'had walked past it four times without stopping'? (Paragraph 4) [1]
questions.answer: that the information they were arguing about had been available all along and nobody had bothered to look

questions.stem: Q5. Explain the meaning of 'A drain is not an enemy.' (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: the mundane real reason gave them nobody to be angry at, which spoilt the satisfaction of their grievance — they had wanted a villain rather than an explanation

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain why the narrator found Ridzuan's telephone call 'extraordinary'. (Paragraph 6) [2]
questions.answer: ① he assumed such a number was meant only for adults to use; ② it had not occurred to him that a child could simply ask an authority for information

questions.stem: Q7. From Paragraph 7, give the TWO reasons why the gate would remain locked after the drain works. [1]
questions.answer: the path crossed land belonging to the block, and someone had complained that children running through early were waking the ground-floor residents

questions.stem: Q8. Using your own words, explain the change in the boys' approach described in Paragraph 9. [2]
questions.answer: ① instead of complaining among themselves they went directly to the people affected; ② they offered something in return by promising to be quiet, treating it as a negotiation rather than a grievance

questions.stem: Q9. What does the old man's behaviour reveal about him? (Paragraph 9) [1]
questions.answer: that he was fair-minded and willing to act on the boys' behalf even though he had no stake in it

questions.stem: Q10. Using your own words, explain why the narrator has 'decided not to believe' Ridzuan's explanation. (Paragraph 11) [1]
questions.answer: he prefers to see the reading of the notice as characteristic of his friend rather than an accident
